front: How is absolute oral bioavailability calculated from oral and IV AUCs?
back: F = (AUC oral / dose oral) ÷ (AUC IV / dose IV).

front: Can a well-absorbed oral drug still have low bioavailability?
back: Yes, because of presystemic gut-wall or hepatic metabolism.
explanation: First-pass metabolism can remove absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: For a weak acid, what happens to ionization as pH rises above pKa?
back: The ionized fraction increases.
explanation: For a weak acid, A−/HA = 10^(pH−pKa) = 100.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What distinguishes facilitated diffusion from active transport?
back: Facilitated diffusion moves down a gradient without energy input.
explanation: Facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated and saturable but does not drive movement against the gradient.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How can shock alter intramuscular drug absorption?
back: Reduced muscle perfusion can make absorption slow and unreliable.
explanation: Poor perfusion slows transfer of an intramuscular dose into systemic circulation.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What is the formula for apparent volume of distribution?
back: Vd = amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma drug concentration.
explanation: Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration = 600/10.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Does a Vd larger than total body water represent an actual fluid compartment?
back: No; it often reflects extensive tissue distribution or binding.
explanation: Vd is a proportionality constant, not a literal anatomical fluid volume.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How is an IV loading dose estimated?
back: Target concentration × volume of distribution.
explanation: Loading dose = target concentration × Vd / F; IV F is 1.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How does strong plasma-protein binding tend to affect Vd, all else equal?
back: It tends to reduce Vd by retaining drug in plasma.
explanation: Greater plasma confinement tends to reduce Vd when other factors are comparable.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What can terminate the effect of a single bolus of a lipid-soluble anesthetic before elimination?
back: Redistribution from the brain to other tissues.
explanation: Movement away from the brain can terminate a single-bolus effect before metabolic elimination is complete.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Which major reaction types are included in phase I metabolism?
back: Oxidation, reduction and hydrolysis.
explanation: Oxidation is a phase I functionalization reaction.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Is glucuronidation a phase I or phase II reaction?
back: Phase II conjugation.
explanation: Glucuronidation attaches glucuronic acid in a conjugation reaction.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How can an enzyme inducer affect an active drug cleared by that enzyme?
back: It can increase clearance and reduce drug exposure.
explanation: Enzyme induction can accelerate metabolism of an active substrate drug.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Why can enzyme inhibition reduce the effectiveness of a prodrug?
back: It may block conversion to the active metabolite.
explanation: Blocking an essential activation step can reduce the effect of a prodrug.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Does drug metabolism always produce inactive metabolites?
back: No; it can produce active metabolites, activate prodrugs or form toxic products.
explanation: Biotransformation can activate a drug rather than invariably inactivate it.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What does a lower EC50 indicate when comparing agonists in the same system?
back: Greater potency.
explanation: Lower EC50 indicates higher potency, while equal maxima indicate equal efficacy in this system.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What distinguishes a partial agonist from a full agonist in the same system?
back: A lower maximal response even at high receptor occupancy.
explanation: A partial agonist has lower intrinsic efficacy than a full agonist in the same system.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What is a quantal drug response?
back: Whether an individual meets a defined yes/no effect endpoint.
explanation: A quantal endpoint records whether a specified effect occurs in each individual.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How is the conventional therapeutic index calculated?
back: TD50 / ED50, using specified therapeutic and toxic endpoints.
explanation: Therapeutic index = 50/5 = 10.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Can a drug be more potent yet less efficacious than another drug?
back: Yes; it can have a lower EC50 but a lower maximal response.
explanation: Potency follows EC50, whereas efficacy follows the achievable maximum in the specified system.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How does a reversible competitive antagonist change a classic agonist response curve?
back: A rightward shift with a preserved maximum.
explanation: Competition lowers apparent agonist potency but can be overcome with sufficient agonist.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What happens to maximal response with an insurmountable noncompetitive antagonist?
back: The attainable maximum decreases.
explanation: An insurmountable signaling blockade reduces the attainable response.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: Why can an irreversible antagonist outlast its presence in plasma?
back: Covalently blocked receptors may remain unavailable until receptor replacement.
explanation: Covalent binding at the agonist site produces persistent receptor blockade.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: What are spare receptors?
back: Receptors beyond the number needed to generate a maximal response in a system.
explanation: A maximal response may require activation of fewer than all available receptors.

references.title: Dr M — source lecture and supplied presentation
IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project
Clinical pharmacokinetics handbook — Ministry of Health Malaysia

front: How can a partial agonist antagonize a full agonist?
back: It occupies the same receptors but produces less activation.
explanation: A partial agonist can antagonize a full agonist by competing for occupancy while producing less activation.
